title: Valid Parentheses
problem: Given a string made only of the characters ()[]{}, decide whether it is valid. A string is valid when every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, and brackets close in the correct order (the most recently opened one must close first).
example: Explanation: "[" closes before "(", "{" opens and closes, then ")" closes the first "(".
intuition: The rule "the most recently opened bracket must close first" is exactly Last-In-First-Out. So keep a stack of open brackets. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; if not (or the stack is empty), the string is invalid. At the end, the stack must be empty, otherwise some bracket was never closed.
A small trick: instead of pushing the opener, push the closer you expect. Then a closing bracket only needs stack.pop() == c.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force keeps deleting adjacent matching pairs until nothing changes, which is O(n²). Since the last opened bracket must close first, a stack fits perfectly: push the expected closer for each opener and check it on each closer. That is O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: empty string (valid), a single character, string starting with a closer like ")(", only openers like " ((", odd length (can return false immediately).
Common mistakes: forgetting the final isEmpty() check; calling pop() on an empty stack; using java.util.Stack (works, but ArrayDeque is the modern choice).

Follow-ups: "Only one bracket type?" Use a counter instead of a stack, O(1) space, and fail if it ever goes negative. "Minimum additions to make it valid?" (LC 921) Same counter idea: count unmatched closers plus leftover openers. 3.2
simple: Do the brackets open and close in the right order?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Any valid string that is non-empty must contain an adjacent pair (), [] or {}.
Repeatedly delete all such adjacent pairs.
Stop when nothing changes. The string was valid only if it became empty.
approaches.why: Each pass is O(n) and removes at least one pair, so there can be up to n/2 passes; each pass builds a new string.
approaches.simple: Keep deleting matching pairs like () [] {} until nothing changes. If the string is empty, it was valid.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Walk the string. For an opener, push the matching closer.
For a closer, if the stack is empty or the popped value is not this closer, return false.
At the end, return whether the stack is empty.
approaches.why: Each character is pushed/popped at most once; in the worst case (all openers) the stack holds n characters.
approaches.simple: Use a stack. Opening bracket: push what should close it. Closing bracket: it must match the top of the stack.

title: Min Stack
problem: Design a stack that supports push(val), pop(), top() and getMin() (return the smallest element currently in the stack). Every operation must run in O(1) time.
example: Explanation: after pushing -2, 0, -3 the min is -3. Pop removes -3, top is 0, min is back to -2.
intuition: The hard part is getMin() after a pop(): if we popped the minimum, what is the new minimum? Notice that a stack never changes "below" the top. So the minimum of the stack at the moment an element was pushed never changes while that element is there. If every entry remembers "the min of everything at or below me", then the answer to getMin() is always stored in the top entry, and popping automatically restores the previous minimum.
Trace: push -2 → (-2, min -2); push 0 → (0, min -2); push -3 → (-3, min -3). Pop → top is (0, min -2). Done.
notes: Say it like this: "A plain stack with a scan gives O(n) getMin. Since nothing below the top changes, each entry can remember the minimum at the time it was pushed, so getMin is just reading the top. All operations become O(1) with O(n) extra space."
Edge cases: duplicate minimums (push -1, -1, pop once; min must still be -1 — the pair approach handles this naturally), negative numbers, Integer.MIN_VALUE.
Common mistakes: with the two-stack variant, pushing to the min stack only when val < min (must be <=, otherwise duplicates break after a pop).

Follow-ups: "Do it with O(1) extra space?" (Striver's version) Store an encoded value: when val < min, push 2*val - min (use long) and set min = val; when popping a value smaller than min, it was encoded, so restore min = 2*min - popped. "Max stack?" Same pair idea with max. 3.3
simple: Build a stack that can also tell you its smallest value instantly.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Use a normal stack (a list).
For getMin(), scan all elements and return the smallest.
approaches.time: O(1) for push/pop/top, O(n) for getMin
approaches.why: The scan visits every element; nothing extra is stored.
approaches.simple: A normal stack; to find the minimum, look through everything.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Store pairs (value, minSoFar) on the stack.
push(val): minSoFar = stack empty? val: min(val, top.minSoFar).
pop(), top() read the top pair; getMin() returns top.minSoFar.
approaches.why: Each operation touches only the top; we store one extra int per element.
approaches.simple: Store each value together with the smallest value at that moment. The top pair always knows the current minimum.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problem: You are given an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish (postfix) notation as an array of tokens. Each token is an integer or one of + - * /. Evaluate it and return the result. Division truncates toward zero, and the input is always valid.
intuition: In postfix, an operator always applies to the two most recent values that have not been used yet. "Most recent" means a stack. Push numbers; when an operator arrives, pop two values, apply the operator, and push the result back because it is now a value that a later operator may use.
Order matters for - and /: the first pop is the right operand, the second pop is the left operand. ["4","2","- "] means 4 - 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Repeatedly reducing the first operator in a list works but is O(n²). An operator always uses the two latest unused values, so a stack does it in one pass: push numbers, pop two on an operator, push the result. O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: negative numbers like "-11" (do not treat "-" prefix as an operator; compare the whole token), single-number input, division of negatives (-7/2 = -3).
Common mistakes: swapping operands for - and /; in JS using Math.floor instead of Math.trunc (wrong for negatives); in JS parseInt on operators.
Follow-ups: "Convert infix to postfix?" Shunting-yard algorithm with an operator stack. "Evaluate an infix string with parentheses?" (Basic Calculator) Use a stack for signs/partial results. 3.4
simple: Work out an expression written in postfix form, like 2 1 + 3 *.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Keep the tokens in a list.
Find the first operator. The two tokens right before it are its operands.
Replace those three tokens with the result and repeat until one token remains.
approaches.why: Each reduction scans from the start and removing from the middle of a list shifts elements; there are up to n/2 reductions.
approaches.simple: Find the first operator, combine the two numbers before it, replace all three with the result, and repeat.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: For each token: if it is a number, push it.
If it is an operator, pop b (right), pop a (left), push a op b.
The single value left on the stack is the answer.
approaches.why: Each token is processed once with O(1) stack work; the stack can hold up to about n/2 numbers.
approaches.simple: Numbers go on a stack. An operator pops two numbers, combines them, and pushes the result.

title: Daily Temperatures
problem: Given daily temperatures, return an array where answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after day i to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future warmer day, answer[i] = 0.
example: Explanation: from 75 (day 2) the next warmer day is 76 on day 6, so wait 4 days.
intuition: This is "next greater element", but we want the distance, so we store indices on the stack. Think of the stack as the list of days still waiting for a warmer day. Their temperatures are in decreasing order from bottom to top (if a later day were warmer, it would already have resolved the earlier one).
When a new day i arrives, every waiting day on top that is colder than temps[i] has just found its answer: i - j. Pop them all, then push i as a new waiting day.
Trace on [73,74,75,71,69,72]: push 0(73). Day1(74) pops 0 → ans[0]=1. Day2(75) pops 1 → ans[1]=1. Push 3(71), 4(69). Day5(72) pops 4 → ans[4]=1, pops 3 → ans[3]=2, stops at 75.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force scans forward from every day, O(n²). This is next-greater-element: I keep a stack of indices still waiting for a warmer day, with decreasing temperatures. A new warmer day pops and answers all colder waiting days. Every index is pushed and popped once, so O(n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: strictly decreasing input (stack keeps all, all answers 0), equal temperatures (not warmer — use strict <), single day.
Common mistakes: pushing values instead of indices (you lose the distance); using <= so equal days wrongly resolve each other.
Follow-ups: "O(1) extra space?" Go right to left and use ans to jump: from j = i+1, while temps[j] <= temps[i], jump j += ans[j] (stop if ans[j] == 0). Amortised O(n). 3.5
simple: For each day, how many days until a warmer day?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each day i, scan forward j = i+1....
Stop at the first j with temps[j] > temps[i]; answer is j - i, else 0.
approaches.why: For a decreasing array every day scans all later days.
approaches.simple: From each day, look forward until you find a warmer one.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep a stack of indices whose temperatures are decreasing (days still waiting).
For each day i: while the stack is non-empty and temps[top] < temps[i], pop j and set ans[j] = i - j.
Push i. Days left on the stack at the end keep answer 0.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner while loop runs n times in total across the whole pass.
approaches.simple: Keep a stack of days still waiting for warmth. A warmer day pops every cooler day off and fills in their answers.

title: Car Fleet
problem: n cars drive toward target on a one-lane road. Car i starts at position[i] with speed speed[i]. A car can never pass the car ahead; if it catches up, it slows down and they move together as one fleet. A car that catches up exactly at the target also joins that fleet. Return how many fleets arrive at the target.
example: Explanation: cars at 10 and 8 meet at 12 (both take 1 hour). The car at 0 arrives alone.
Cars at 5 and 3 meet at 6 and arrive together. So 3 fleets.
intuition: Forget the actual collisions. For each car compute the time it would need to reach the target if the road were empty: time = (target - position) / speed. Now look at cars from the one closest to the target backwards. A car behind cannot overtake, so if its time is less than or equal to the time of the fleet just ahead of it, it catches up and merges (its real time becomes the fleet's time). If its time is greater, it is too slow to catch up and it starts a new fleet, which becomes the new "fleet ahead".
So after sorting by position descending, the number of fleets equals the number of times the time strictly increases past the current maximum.
Trace (sorted by position): pos 10 t=1 → fleet (max=1). pos 8 t=1 → merges. pos 5 t=7 → new fleet (max=7). pos 3 t=3 → merges. pos 0 t=12 → new fleet. Total 3.
notes: Say it like this: "I convert each car into its solo arrival time. Brute force checks for each car whether any car ahead is slower or equal, O(n²). Sorting by position descending, a car starts a new fleet only if its time exceeds the time of the fleet ahead, so one pass after sorting gives O(n log n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: one car (1 fleet), cars that meet exactly at the target (same time → same fleet, so use strict >), all cars with the same time.
Common mistakes: integer division for time; sorting ascending and scanning the wrong way; trying to simulate positions hour by hour.

Follow-ups: "Can you avoid floating point?" Compare (target-p1)*s2 vs (target-p2)*s1 using long. "Can it be O(n)?" If positions are bounded by target, bucket cars by position (counting sort) and scan from target down. 3.6
simple: Cars drive to a target; a faster car that catches a slower one joins it as a fleet. How many fleets arrive?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Compute each car's solo time.
Car i leads its own fleet only if no car in front of it (larger position) has time >= time[i]; such a car would block it.
Count cars that are not blocked, checking all pairs (no sorting needed).
approaches.why: For each car we look at every other car; we store n times.
approaches.simple: Compute each car's arrival time and check for each car whether someone ahead would block it.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Pair up (position, time) and sort by position descending.
Keep maxTime = arrival time of the fleet directly ahead (start at 0).
For each car: if time > maxTime, it is a new fleet: fleets++, maxTime = time. Otherwise it merges. This is a monotonic stack where we only ever need the top, so a single variable replaces the stack.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the scan is O(n). We store the pairs.
approaches.simple: Sort cars from closest to the target. A car that would arrive later than the fleet ahead starts a new fleet; otherwise it joins.

title: Largest Rectangle In Histogram
problem: Given an array heights where each bar has width 1, return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.
example: Explanation: bars 5 and 6 (indices 2..3) give height 5 × width 2 = 10.
intuition: Every candidate rectangle is limited by its shortest bar. So flip the question: for each bar i, what is the widest rectangle in which heights[i] is the shortest bar? It stretches left until the first bar shorter than it (previous smaller element) and right until the first bar shorter than it (next smaller element). Area = heights[i] * (right - left - 1).

Previous/next smaller elements are exactly what a monotonic increasing stack gives. Keep indices with increasing heights. When bar i is shorter than the top, the top bar has just found its right boundary (i), and the element below it on the stack is its left boundary. Pop and compute its area right then. At the end, use i = n as a sentinel "height 0" bar so every remaining bar gets popped.
Trace on [2,1,5,6,2,3]: push 0. i=1 (h=1) pops 0: width = 1 → area 2. Push 1, 2, 3. i=4 (h=2) pops 3 (h=6): left=2, width=4-2-1=1 → 6; pops 2 (h=5): left=1, width=4-1-1=2 → 10.... Max 10.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every left and right edge with a running minimum, O(n²). Instead, each bar is the shortest bar of the widest rectangle bounded by its previous and next smaller bars. A monotonic increasing stack finds both boundaries at pop time, so I get the answer in one pass, O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: single bar, all equal heights (popping on >= still gives the right width for the last equal bar), strictly increasing (everything is popped by the sentinel), zeros.
Common mistakes: forgetting the final flush (sentinel at i = n); using i - top as width instead of i - newTop - 1; storing heights instead of indices.

Follow-ups: "Explain the two-pass version" (Striver): compute pse[] and nse[] arrays with two monotonic stack passes, then area = h[i] * (nse[i] - pse[i] - 1). Same O(n), easier to explain, more memory. "2D version?" Maximal Rectangle (3.13) runs this on each row. 3.7
simple: Find the largest rectangle that fits under the histogram bars.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Fix the left edge i.
Extend the right edge j from i to the end, keeping the running minimum height.
Area of [i..j] is minHeight * (j - i + 1); track the max.
approaches.why: All O(n²) pairs (i, j) are visited, and the running minimum makes each step O(1).
approaches.simple: Fix a left edge, extend to the right keeping the lowest bar, and compute areas.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights.
For i = 0..n (treat heights[n] as 0): while the stack is non-empty and heights[top] >= h, pop top.
For the popped bar: right boundary is i, left boundary is the new top (or -1 if empty). Width = i - left - 1. Update the answer with heights[top] * width.
Push i.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed and popped once; the stack can hold all n indices for an increasing array.
approaches.simple: Keep a stack of bars with rising heights. When a lower bar arrives, pop taller ones and measure the rectangle each popped bar could make.

title: Next Greater Element
problem: Given an array arr, for every element find the next greater element: the first element to its right that is strictly larger. If there is none, use -1. (This is the GFG/Striver version. LeetCode 496 asks the same thing for a subset of values; solve it with this and a hash map.)
example: Explanation: next greater of 4 is 5, of 5 is 25, of 2 is 25, nothing is greater than 25.
intuition: Scan from the right. Keep a stack of candidates that could be "next greater" for elements further left. When you stand at arr[i], any candidate <= arr[i] is useless forever: arr[i] is both closer and at least as big for every element to the left. So pop them. Whatever remains on top is the next greater element of arr[i] (or the stack is empty → -1). Then push arr[i] as a candidate.
The stack is always decreasing from bottom to top. That is the monotonic stack.
Trace on [4,5,2,25] from right: 25 → stack empty → -1, push 25. 2 → top 25 → 25, push 2. 5 → pop 2, top 25 → 25, push 5. 4 → top 5 → 5.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force scans right for each element, O(n²). Going right to left, any candidate not bigger than the current element can never be an answer again, so I pop it. The stack stays decreasing and its top is the answer. Each element is pushed and popped once: O(n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: duplicates (strictly greater, so pop on <=), all equal (all -1), decreasing array, single element.
Common mistakes: popping on < (then equal elements become each other's answer); reading the top before popping.

Follow-ups: "LeetCode 496 (nums1 subset of nums2)?" Run this on nums2, store value → next greater in a map, answer queries for nums1. "Previous greater / next smaller?" Change the scan direction or the comparison; the template is the same. 3.8
simple: For each number, find the first bigger number to its right.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each i, scan j = i+1....
The first arr[j] > arr[i] is the answer; otherwise -1.
approaches.why: For a decreasing array every element scans to the end.
approaches.simple: Scan right from each number until something bigger shows up.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Go from i = n-1 down to 0 with an empty stack.
Pop while top <= arr[i].
ans[i] = stack empty? -1: top. Push arr[i].
approaches.why: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once.
approaches.simple: Walk from the right with a stack. Pop anything not bigger than the current number; the top that remains is the answer.

title: Next Greater Element - 2
problem: Same as Next Greater Element, but the array is circular: after the last element we wrap to the first. For each element, return the first strictly greater element in circular order, or -1 if none exists.
example: Explanation: the last 3 wraps around and finds 4. 4 is the max, so -1.
intuition: Circular means "pretend the array is written twice": [1,2,3,4,3,1,2,3,4,3]. The next greater element of index i in the circular array is the next greater of i in this doubled array. We do not need to build it; index i % n gives the value.
So run the right-to-left monotonic stack over indices 2n-1... 0. The first pass (indices n..2n-1) just fills the stack with candidates that sit "after the wrap". Only record answers when i < n.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks the next n-1 circular positions for each element, O(n²). Circular is the same as the array concatenated with itself, so I run the next-greater monotonic stack over 2n virtual indices using i % n, recording answers only for the first n. O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: all equal (all -1), single element (-1), the maximum element (always -1), duplicates of the max.
Common mistakes: actually copying the array (works but wastes memory); writing answers for i >= n (index out of bounds); iterating only n times.
Follow-ups: "Return the distance instead of the value?" Store indices on the stack and compute (j - i + n) % n. "Next smaller in a circular array?" Flip the comparison. 3.9
simple: Next bigger number to the right, but the list wraps around in a circle.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each i, check the next n-1 positions (i+1)%n, (i+2)%n,....
The first strictly greater value is the answer; otherwise -1.
approaches.why: Each element may check all other n-1 elements.
approaches.simple: From each number, check the next n − 1 positions going around the circle.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: For i from 2n-1 down to 0, let x = nums[i % n].
Pop while top <= x.
If i < n, ans[i] = stack empty? -1: top.
Push x.
approaches.why: 2n iterations, and each pushed value is popped at most once; the stack holds at most n useful values at a time.
approaches.simple: Pretend the list is written twice and use the same stack trick from the right.

title: Stock span problem
problem: Design StockSpanner (LeetCode 901, Online Stock Span). next(price) receives today's price and returns its span: the number of consecutive days, ending today and going backwards, on which the price was less than or equal to today's price (today counts).
example: Input:    next(100), next(80), next(60), next(70), next(60), next(75), next(85)
Explanation: for 75 the days 60, 70, 60, 75 are all <= 75, so the span is 4.
intuition: The span ends at the previous greater element: the last earlier day with a strictly higher price. Everything between that day and today is <= today.

Keep a stack of (price, span) with prices strictly decreasing. When today's price arrives, every stack entry with price <= today is swallowed: today's span absorbs their spans (those days and everything they had already swallowed are all <= today). Pop them and add their spans. Push (price, totalSpan).
notes: Say it like this: "Walking back each day is O(n) per call. The span stops at the previous greater price, so I keep a decreasing stack of (price, span); a new price pops all smaller-or-equal entries and adds their spans. Every day is pushed and popped once, so amortised O(1) per call and O(n) space."
Edge cases: strictly increasing prices (stack keeps collapsing to one entry; span = day number), strictly decreasing (every span 1), equal prices (<= so they are absorbed).
Common mistakes: using < instead of <=; returning span but forgetting to push today.

Follow-ups: "Array version (GFG)?" Same logic with indices: span[i] = i - prevGreaterIndex, where the previous greater index is the stack top after popping (or -1). "Why amortised O(1)?" Total pops ≤ total pushes = n. 3.10
simple: Each day, report how many consecutive days (including today) had a price at most today's.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Store all prices in a list.
On next(price), add it, then walk backwards counting while the price is <= today's.
approaches.why: For an increasing price series each call walks back over all previous days.
approaches.simple: Store all prices and walk backwards counting each time.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep a stack of [price, span] with strictly decreasing prices.
On next(price): span = 1; while top price <= price, span += pop().span.
Push [price, span] and return span.
approaches.why: Each day is pushed once and popped at most once over all calls.
approaches.simple: Keep a stack of (price, span). Today's price swallows smaller days and adds their spans to its own.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
problem: Given an integer array arr, find the sum of min(subarray) over every contiguous subarray. Return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7.
intuition: There are O(n²) subarrays, so listing them is too slow. Flip the view: instead of asking "what is the min of each subarray", ask "in how many subarrays is arr[i] the minimum?" (the contribution technique). Then the answer is Σ arr[i] × count[i].

arr[i] is the minimum of a subarray [L..R] if the subarray does not reach past the nearest smaller element on either side. Let left[i] = number of choices for the start L (distance from i back to the previous smaller element) and right[i] = number of choices for the end R (distance to the next smaller element). Then count[i] = left[i] × right[i]. Both distances come from monotonic stacks.

Duplicates trap: in [2,2], the subarray [2,2] must be counted for exactly one of the two 2s. So be strict on one side and non-strict on the other: left boundary = previous strictly smaller, right boundary = next smaller or equal.

Check on [3,1,2,4]: for the 1 at index 1, left = 2 (start at 0 or 1), right = 3 (end at 1, 2 or 3), so it contributes 1 × 6 = 6. 3 contributes 3×1, 2 contributes 2×(1×2)=4, 4 contributes 4×1. Total 3+6+4+4 = 17.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force enumerates all subarrays with a running min, O(n²). Instead I count, for each element, how many subarrays it is the minimum of: left choices times right choices, bounded by the previous and next smaller elements, which two monotonic stack passes give in O(n). I use strict on one side and non-strict on the other so duplicates are counted once."
Edge cases: duplicates (the strict/non-strict split), single element, all equal values, large n (use long in Java, BigInt or careful modding in JS).
Common mistakes: strict on both sides (undercounts) or non-strict on both (double counts); overflow in arr[i] * left * right.

Follow-ups: "Sum of subarray maximums?" Same thing with greater instead of smaller. That leads directly to Sum of Subarray Ranges (3.11). "One pass?" Possible: compute both boundaries when an index is popped (its right boundary is the popper, left is the new top). 3.11
simple: Add up the minimum of every continuous piece of the list.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Fix the start i.
Extend the end j to the right, keeping the running minimum.
Add the running minimum for each (i, j).
approaches.why: Every subarray is visited once and its min is updated in O(1).
approaches.simple: Try every piece, keeping a running minimum, and add it.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Left-to-right with a stack of indices: pop while arr[top] >= arr[i]; then left[i] = empty? i+1: i - top (top is the previous strictly smaller).
Right-to-left: pop while arr[top] > arr[i]; then right[i] = empty? n-i: top - i (top is the next smaller-or-equal).
Answer = Σ arr[i] × left[i] × right[i] mod 1e9+7, computed in long.
approaches.why: Two passes, each index pushed and popped once per pass; three arrays/stacks of size n.
approaches.simple: For each number, count how many pieces it is the minimum of (using nearest smaller on each side), and add number × count.

title: Sum of Subarray Ranges
problem: The range of a subarray is max - min. Given nums, return the sum of ranges over all contiguous subarrays.
intuition: Σ (max - min) = Σ max - Σ min. We just learned how to compute the sum of subarray minimums in O(n) by counting each element's contribution (3.10). The sum of subarray maximums is the same trick with comparisons flipped: element i is the maximum of left × right subarrays, where the boundaries are the previous strictly greater and the next greater-or-equal elements.
So the problem is two calls to the same helper.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tracks running min and max for all subarrays, O(n²). The sum of ranges equals the sum of maximums minus the sum of minimums, and each of those is a contribution count from monotonic stacks: element times left choices times right choices. That gives O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: single element (0), all equal (0), negative numbers (the formula still holds), large values (use long).
Common mistakes: inconsistent tie handling between the two passes; overflow when multiplying a[i] * left * right in int.

Follow-ups: "Why does the tie rule matter?" Without strict on one side, a subarray with two equal minima is counted twice. "Can you do it with one stack per sum?" Yes, compute contribution at pop time. 3.12
simple: Add up (max − min) over every continuous piece of the list.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Fix the start i, extend the end j, maintaining running min and max.
Add max - min for each subarray.
approaches.why: All subarrays visited with O(1) update each. (This passes LeetCode's n ≤ 1000, but the interviewer will ask for O(n).)
approaches.simple: Try every piece with a running min and max.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Write one helper contribution(nums, isMax) that returns the sum of subarray minimums (or maximums).
For minimums: left boundary = previous strictly smaller, right = next smaller-or-equal. For maximums: flip </>.
Return sumMax - sumMin as a long.
approaches.why: Four monotonic stack passes in total, each linear.
approaches.simple: Sum of all maximums minus sum of all minimums, each computed with the monotonic stack trick.

title: Remove K Digits
problem: Given a non-negative integer as a string num and an integer k, remove exactly k digits so that the remaining number is as small as possible. Return it as a string without leading zeros (return "0" if nothing is left).
intuition: Numbers with the same length are compared from the left, so the most important thing is to make the leftmost digits as small as possible. Greedy rule: if a digit is bigger than the digit right after it, removing it makes the number smaller (the smaller next digit moves into a more significant position). So we want the result to be non-decreasing as far as our k removals allow.

That is a monotonic increasing stack. Push digits; before pushing d, while we still have removals and the top is greater than d, pop it (that is one removal). If removals are left at the end, the stack is non-decreasing, so drop digits from the end (the largest ones). Finally strip leading zeros.
Trace "1432219", k=3: push 1, push 4; 3 pops 4 (k=2), push 3; 2 pops 3 (k=1), push 2; 2 push; 1 pops 2 (k=0), push 1; push 9. Stack = 1 2 1 9 → "1219".
notes: Say it like this: "Leftmost digits matter most, so whenever a digit is bigger than the next one I should remove it. Doing that one removal at a time is O(n·k). A monotonic increasing stack does all removals in one pass: pop bigger digits while k lasts, trim the end if k is left, strip leading zeros. O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: k == num.length() → "0"; result with leading zeros like "10200", k=1 → "200"; non- decreasing input like "12345" (remove from the end); all zeros.
Common mistakes: forgetting to use up leftover k; not stripping leading zeros; returning "" instead of "0".
Follow-ups: "Largest number instead?" Flip the comparison (decreasing stack). "Smallest subsequence of length m?" Same as removing n - m digits. Related: Remove Duplicate Letters (LC 316). 3.13
simple: Remove k digits to make the smallest possible number.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Repeat k times: scan for the first index i with num[i] > num[i+1] and delete it; if the string is non-decreasing, delete the last digit.
Strip leading zeros; return "0" if empty.
approaches.why: Each of the k deletions rescans from the start and shifts characters. (Truly brute force — trying all C(n,k) subsets — is exponential; this greedy one-at-a-time version is the natural first answer.)
approaches.simple: k times, remove the first digit that is bigger than the next one.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Use a StringBuilder / array as a stack.
For each digit d: while k > 0, stack non-empty and top > d, pop and k--. Push d.
While k > 0, pop from the end.
Skip leading zeros; return "0" if empty.
approaches.why: Each digit is pushed and popped at most once.
approaches.simple: Use a stack: while the last kept digit is bigger than the new one and you still can remove, drop it. Keeps digits as small as possible from the left.

title: Maximum Rectangles
problem: (LeetCode 85, Maximal Rectangle.) Given a binary matrix of '0' and '1' characters, find the largest rectangle containing only '1' s and return its area.
example: Explanation: rows 1–2, columns 2–4 form a 2 × 3 block of ones.
intuition: Fix the bottom row of the rectangle. For each column, count how many consecutive '1' s stand on top of each other ending at this row: that is a histogram. Any all-ones rectangle whose bottom edge is on this row is a rectangle in this histogram. So the answer is the max over all rows of "Largest Rectangle in Histogram" (3.6).
Heights are easy to update row by row: h[j] = matrix[i][j] == '1'? h[j] + 1: 0.
For the example, row 2 gives heights [3,1,3,2,2]; the best rectangle there is height 2 × width 3 = 6.
notes: Say it like this: "Treating every cell as a bottom-right corner and walking upward with a min width is O(r²·c). If I fix the bottom row, the column heights of consecutive ones form a histogram, so I run Largest Rectangle in Histogram on each row. That is O(r·c) time and O(c) space."
Edge cases: all zeros (0), a single row or column, matrix of all ones (r × c), char vs int input (LeetCode uses '1' chars).
Common mistakes: forgetting to reset the height to 0 on a '0'; comparing matrix[i][j] == 1 instead of '1'.
Follow-ups: "Largest square of ones?" (LC 221) Simpler DP: dp[i][j] = 1 + min(top, left, top-left). "Count all submatrices of ones?" (LC 1504) Histogram + monotonic stack counting. 3.14
simple: In a grid of 0s and 1s, find the largest rectangle of only 1s.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Precompute width[i][j] = number of consecutive '1' s ending at (i, j) going left.
Treat every cell (i, j) as the bottom-right corner. Walk upward row by row k = i, i-1,..., keeping minWidth = min(width[k][j]).
The rectangle with rows k..i ending at column j has area minWidth × (i - k + 1); stop when minWidth hits 0.
approaches.why: Each of the r·c cells walks up at most r rows; the width table has r·c entries.
approaches.simple: Treat every cell as a bottom-right corner and grow upward, tracking how wide the rectangle can stay.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep heights[c], initially zeros.
For each row, update heights[j] (+1 for '1', reset to 0 for '0').
Run the monotonic-stack largest-rectangle routine on heights and track the max.
approaches.why: Each row costs O(cols) to update and O(cols) for the stack pass; we store one heights array and one stack.
approaches.simple: Turn each row into a histogram of how many 1s stack up above it, then reuse Largest Rectangle in Histogram on each row.

title: Asteroid Collision
problem: Each integer in asteroids is an asteroid in a row: the absolute value is its size, the sign is its direction (positive = right, negative = left). All move at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one explodes; if equal, both explode. Asteroids moving in the same direction never meet. Return the state after all collisions.
example: Explanation: 10 and -5 collide, 10 survives. 5 and 10 move right and never meet.
intuition: A collision happens only when a right-moving asteroid is to the left of a left-moving one (+ then -). A new left- moving asteroid will first hit the nearest surviving right-mover before it, then the next one, and so on. "Nearest surviving one before me" is the top of a stack.

So keep the survivors on a stack. For a new asteroid a: while a < 0 and the top is positive, compare sizes. If the top is smaller, it explodes (pop) and a keeps going. If equal, both explode. If the top is bigger, a explodes. If a survives all fights, push it.
Trace [10,2,-5]: push 10, push 2. -5 vs 2 → pop 2. -5 vs 10 → -5 explodes. Result [10].
notes: Say it like this: "Repeatedly resolving the first colliding pair is O(n²). A left-mover always hits the nearest surviving right-mover first, which is the stack top, so I simulate with a stack: pop smaller right-movers, handle equal sizes, push if it survives. Each asteroid is pushed and popped once: O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: [-2,-1,1,2] (no collisions — negatives on the left move away), equal sizes [8,-8] → [], a big negative clearing the whole stack, all positive.
Common mistakes: treating (-, +) as a collision (they move apart); forgetting the equal case; pushing the negative asteroid after it already exploded.
Follow-ups: "Return how many survive?" Return the stack size. "Different speeds?" It becomes an event simulation with a priority queue by collision time, much harder. 3.15
simple: Asteroids move left or right; when they meet, the smaller explodes. What is left?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Keep the asteroids in a list.
Find the first adjacent pair (+, -). Resolve it (remove the smaller, or both if equal).
Repeat until no such pair exists.
approaches.why: Each pass scans from the start and each removal from the middle of a list is O(n); there can be up to n collisions.
approaches.simple: Keep finding a right-mover followed by a left-mover, resolve that crash, and repeat.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Stack of survivors.
For each a: set alive = true. While alive, a < 0, and top > 0: - top < -a: pop, continue. - top == -a: pop, alive = false. - top > -a: alive = false.
If alive, push a. The stack (bottom to top) is the answer.
approaches.why: Each asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once.
approaches.simple: Use a stack of survivors. A left-mover crashes into right-movers on top of the stack until it dies or nothing blocks it.

title: Celebrity Problem
problem: At a party of n people (0 to n-1), a celebrity is someone who is known by everyone else but knows no one. You are given an n × n matrix where mat[i][j] = 1 means person i knows person j. Return the celebrity's index, or -1 if there is none. (This is the Striver/GFG version; LeetCode 277 "Find the Celebrity" is the same with a knows(a, b) API instead of the matrix.)
example: Explanation: person 1 knows nobody (row 1 is all 0) and everyone else knows 1 (column 1 is 1 elsewhere).
intuition: One question knows(a, b) always rules someone out: - If a knows b, then a is not a celebrity (celebrities know no one). - If a does not know b, then b is not a celebrity (everyone must know a celebrity).

So each comparison eliminates exactly one person. After n - 1 comparisons, one candidate is left. It is the only possible celebrity, but not guaranteed, so verify it with one more O(n) check of its row and column.
There can be at most one celebrity: if two existed, each would have to know the other, contradicting "knows no one".
notes: Say it like this: "Checking every person's row and column is O(n²). Each knows(a, b) query eliminates one person, so n-1 queries leave a single candidate, which I verify in O(n). With a stack that is O(n) space; with two pointers from both ends it is O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: no celebrity (verification fails → -1), n = 1 (that person is the celebrity), diagonal values of 1 (some GFG versions say a person knows themselves — always skip j == i).
Common mistakes: skipping the verification step (the survivor is only a candidate); not ignoring the diagonal.

Follow-ups: "Minimise calls to knows()?" Elimination uses n-1 calls, verification at most 2(n-1); you can skip re- asking pairs already asked during elimination. "Why at most one celebrity?" Two celebrities would have to know each other. 3.16
simple: A celebrity is known by everyone but knows nobody. Find them, if they exist.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each person i, check row i: they must know nobody (ignoring j == i).
Check column i: everyone else must know them.
Return the first i that passes, else -1.
approaches.why: For each of n people we read one full row and one full column.
approaches.simple: Check every person: nobody in their row, everybody in their column.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Push all people onto a stack.
While more than one remains: pop a and b. If a knows b, push b; else push a (the eliminated one is dropped).
Verify the remaining candidate's row and column.
approaches.why: n-1 eliminations plus an O(n) verification; the stack holds n people.
approaches.simple: Put everyone on a stack. Pop two: whoever knows the other can't be the celebrity. Check the last one left.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Two pointers top = 0, down = n - 1.
While top < down: if top knows down, top++ (top is out); else down-- (down is out).
Candidate is top. Verify its row and column.
approaches.why: Each step removes one person from the range; verification is one row and one column.
approaches.simple: Two pointers at both ends. One question eliminates one person. Check the survivor.

title: LFU Cache
problem: Design a Least Frequently Used cache with a fixed capacity. get(key) returns the value (or -1) and counts as a use. put(key, value) inserts or updates and also counts as a use. When the cache is full and a new key arrives, evict the key with the lowest use count; break ties by evicting the least recently used among them. Both operations must be O(1) on average.
example: Explanation: get(1) makes freq(1)=2. put(3) evicts key 2 (freq 1). get(3) makes freq(3)=2.
put(4): keys 1 and 3 both have freq 2; key 1 was used less recently, so evict 1.
intuition: We need two orderings at once: by frequency, and within the same frequency by recency. Group keys into buckets by frequency. Inside each bucket keep keys in recency order (oldest first): that is just an LRU list per frequency. Also track minFreq, the smallest frequency present.

Using a key moves it from bucket f to the end of bucket f+1. If bucket f becomes empty and f == minFreq, then minFreq = f + 1. Evicting removes the first (oldest) key from bucket minFreq. A brand-new key goes into bucket 1 and sets minFreq = 1.

In Java, LinkedHashSet is a ready-made "ordered set with O(1) add/remove"; in JavaScript, Set keeps insertion order too. (In a no-library interview, each bucket is a doubly linked list exactly like LRU Cache.)
notes: Say it like this: "A single map with frequency and timestamp works but eviction scans everything, O(n). For O(1), I group keys into frequency buckets, each an LRU-ordered list, plus a minFreq pointer. A use moves a key from bucket f to f+1, eviction takes the oldest key in the minFreq bucket, and a new key resets minFreq to 1. All operations are O(1) average with O(capacity) space."

Edge cases: capacity == 0 (put does nothing, get returns -1), updating an existing key (counts as a use, no eviction), ties in frequency (evict least recent), get of a missing key must not change anything.

Common mistakes: evicting after inserting the new key (you might evict the new key itself); forgetting to bump minFreq when its bucket empties during touch; forgetting that put on an existing key increases the frequency.

Follow-ups: "Why does minFreq never need a search?" It only changes in two ways: a new key sets it to 1, and touching the last key of bucket minFreq moves that key to minFreq + 1, so the new minimum is exactly minFreq + 1. "Implement without LinkedHashSet?" Each bucket becomes a doubly linked list with head/tail sentinels and the map stores node references, exactly like LRU Cache. "LRU vs LFU?" LRU only tracks recency; LFU keeps popular items even if they were not used very recently.
simple: Build a cache that, when full, throws out the least frequently used key (ties: the oldest).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Map key → {value, freq, lastUsedTime} with a global clock.
get / put of an existing key: update value, freq++, lastUsedTime = ++clock.
When full, scan all entries to find the smallest (freq, lastUsedTime) and remove it.
approaches.time: get O(1), put O(capacity) when evicting
approaches.why: Eviction scans every entry; storage is one record per key.
approaches.simple: Store frequency and last-used time per key; to evict, scan all keys for the worst one.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: vals: key → {value, freq}; buckets: freq → ordered set of keys (oldest first); minFreq.
touch(key): remove key from buckets[f]; if that bucket is empty, delete it and, if f == minFreq, set minFreq = f+1. Add key to the end of buckets[f+1]; freq = f+1.
get: missing → -1; else touch and return the value.
put: if capacity == 0 return. Existing key → update value, touch. New key → if full, remove the first key of buckets[minFreq] from both maps; insert with freq 1 into buckets[1]; minFreq = 1.
approaches.time: O(1) average for get and put
approaches.why: Every step is a hash-map lookup or an O(1) ordered-set add/remove; we store each key once in vals and once in a bucket.
approaches.simple: Group keys into buckets by frequency, each bucket ordered by age, and track the lowest frequency. Eviction is just taking the oldest key from that bucket.
